title: Desurvire, Caplan, Toth, Using Heuristics to Evaluate the Playability of Games (CHI 2004 late-breaking results)
label: research
claim: HEP game-play heuristic: "Provide clear goals, present overriding goal early as well as short-term goals throughout play." Mechanics heuristic 3: "A player should always be able to identify their score/status and goal in the game." Also Game Play 13 "The first player action is painfully obvious". Late-breaking comparison of HEP vs user studies; says nothing about hidden gates or reward disclosure specifically. Heuristics are authors' adaptation of productivity-software heuristics, not an empirical ranking.

title: Microsoft, Xbox Accessibility Guideline 109 (XAG, Xbox devdocs)
label: guideline
claim: "Players can review current tasks and objectives at any time"; log "ideally separated by main vs side quests"; players should be able to look up "What they should do next"; optional "waypoint or path markers, hints, and directional cues" when the player has made no progress. Supports showing the current objective and marking the main track (main/side separation is in the completed-log, 'ideally'). Does not require a hidden gate be disclosed, nor say anything on rewards.

title: Game Accessibility Guidelines, Indicate / allow reminder of current objectives during gameplay (Cognitive, intermediate)
label: guideline
claim: "A reminder can help greatly." Shown "permanently displayed, on player request, or triggered automatically". Examples: Assassin's Creed Syndicate wayfinding, Doom wayfinding, Silence hints, Skyrim objective summary. Level intermediate. Only about reminders of current objective; silent on main vs side and on reward text.

title: Golubeva (Ice-Pick Lodge narrative designer), Pathologic 2 mindmap: a quest log people actually read (Game Developer, GDC-style talk transcript)
label: developer
claim: COUNTEREXAMPLE to marking the main track and showing what remains: "Get rid of the idea of 'main' and 'side' quests" and "we do not reveal how many such nodes are ahead"; there is "another circle, still invisible". Developer deliberately hides how much remains and does not mark a main track. Speaks for one game; says the author notes it may not suit every game. Shows hidden extent paired with a visible record of what happened (mindmap), not a bare hidden gate.

title: gamedev.net, 7 UX Lessons From The Trenches
label: snippet
claim: Seen only in search summary: team found many players skipped on-screen prompts, "most serious impact when they missed instructions about what to do next". One team's case notes, not a ranking across studies.

title: Games User Research book material, Designing a games user research study
label: snippet
claim: Seen only in search summary: example study question 'Will players know where to go for their next objective?' measured by observing behaviour. Frames objective clarity as a standard research question; does NOT say it is the top finding.

title: Pinelle, Wong, Stach, Heuristic evaluation for games: usability principles for video game design (CHI 2008)
label: snippet
claim: Confirmed to exist: ten heuristics from categorized game-review usability problems; five evaluators, one PC demo. I could NOT read the heuristic wording, so no claim about a goals heuristic is made here; the later full-read Pinelle row supersedes this one.

title: Loewenstein, The Psychology of Curiosity: A Review and Reinterpretation (Psychological Bulletin 116(1), 1994)
label: snippet
claim: Abstract as seen via search: curiosity as "cognitively induced deprivation" from perceiving "a gap in knowledge or understanding". Does NOT address games, locked entries, or whether showing a condition while hiding a reward preserves surprise; applying it that way is inference.

title: Tang & Kirman, Exploring Curiosity in Games: A Framework and Questionnaire Study of Player Perspectives (Int. J. Human-Computer Interaction, 2024)
read: full text extracted (pdftotext), grepped not read end-to-end
label: research
claim: Questionnaire study; players prefer games that "strike a delicate balance between uncertainty and the anticipation of future rewards". Notes practitioners "conflat[e]" curiosity with exploration and treat it as simple Loewenstein information-gap. Says hidden missions/treasures can facilitate exploratory curiosity. Does NOT test hiding a reward while showing its condition. Closest peer-reviewed game-curiosity source found; indirect for showing a gate's condition while hiding its reward.

title: Steam/Choice of Games/PC Gamer/Kotaku forum threads on hidden achievements (several)
label: snippet
claim: Seen only in search summaries: mixed anecdotes. Hidden achievements accepted when they reward discovery; one reviewer found 14 hidden achievements in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter 'really unfair' and suggested hiding them only until a first playthrough ends. Steam hidden achievements reveal only once earned (by design). No survey data.

title: itch.io / Steam comments on idle games (Midnight Idle, Smashing Simulator Idle, Atom Idle)
label: snippet
claim: Seen only in search summaries: players say they had "no idea how to open the doors" (Midnight Idle) and ask how to unlock the tech store / 'unclear how to progress' (Smashing Simulator Idle). Anecdotal player complaints about unclear gates; could not tell verbatim wording from summary, so not quoted as verbatim.

title: null result: Hodent Gamer's Brain on clear goals; BotW/Elden Ring developer statements on markers; Nielsen visibility in game context
label: null
claim: Queries: 'Hodent The Gamers Brain clear goals signs and feedback...'; 'Kao curiosity game hidden reward condition... Elden Ring OR Breath of the Wild quest log'; 'Breath of the Wild developers interview shrine marker Fujibayashi Aonuma triangle...'. No page with Hodent's wording on goals found (only foreword/blog); no dev statement on BotW guidance without markers found; Elden Ring item was a syndicated article with an unnamed-game quote, unverified. Kao et al. not found. No source found on showing-gate-hiding-reward specifically.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, 10 Usability Heuristics: #1 Visibility of System Status (nngroup.com, undated page; heuristic from Nielsen 1994)
read: full (fetched page, summarized by fetch tool)
label: guideline
claim: "The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback" within a reasonable time; "When users know the current system status, they learn the outcome of their prior interactions and determine next steps." Says no action with consequences should happen without informing the user. General UI heuristic; does NOT mention games or timers.

title: Chris Avellone, Challenge vs Frustration: Bloggin' on Time Limits (Obsidian Forums blog, 2012-05-18)
label: practitioner
claim: Avellone likes time limits for urgency; says Fallout 1's water chip deadline suited its world but players disliked it as unforgiving and discouraging of leisurely exploration. Cites System Shock 2 as a better model: "It was forgiving. When the time limit ran out, you would be inconvenienced, not fail the game" while still making you "keep an eye on the clock". Post does NOT say whether the water chip timer was on screen. Commenter WorstUsernameEver (label opinion, unverified) claims Fallout had a second hidden timer for the Super Mutant invasion, removed by patch after player objections; Silver6986 values visible reminders (Fallout 2 dream sequences).

title: GOG forum threads on the Fallout 1 time limit; Doomworld and RPG Codex discussion (various, undated)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary only: players report the 150-day water chip limit was criticised as off-putting, but the remaining time is visible in the Pipboy and the game reminds the player from the 50-day mark. So Fallout's chip timer is evidence for a visible-but-disliked timer, not a hidden one. Sources disagree on whether the limit was patched out. Not read; do not cite as a hidden-timer complaint.

title: GameSpot, Why Dead Rising 4's Campaign Ditches the Series' Most Divisive Mechanic (2016)
label: snippet
claim: Search result summaries from GameSpot, GodIsAGeek, CGMagazine, TweakTown say Capcom dropped the timer in DR4 because it kept players from finding side content (developers: with a timer players couldn't finish half the side content they wanted). Dead Rising 1 shows a colored case gauge top right; DR2 shows timers on HUD. These sources describe a visible timer that was divisive, NOT a hidden one. Page itself unread.

title: Stardew Valley Wiki, Random Events / Strange Capsule / child event (community wiki)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary: Stardew's child event fires about two weeks (14 days) after the player agrees, and the Strange Capsule breaks after a few days then triggers an event 'if you know where to look'. Examples of progress gated on unseen delays in a game, but no complaint or developer statement was found. Animal Crossing and Pikmin searches returned nothing relevant.

title: Zelda Dungeon / Game Informer and Iwata Asks coverage, Majora's Mask three-day cycle design (2015 interviews as reported)
label: snippet
claim: Reported Aonuma explanation: returning to day one made players think they'd go through an entire week again, so "three days would be just right". Fetch of the Game Developer interview page (gamedeveloper.com Aonuma / Miyamoto challenge) found NO mention of the on-screen clock or time visibility; that page only describes the Three-Day System concept. So no developer statement on timer visibility was found for Majora's Mask.

title: Know Your Meme, Game devs remind gamers that they are 'very dumb' after signposting discourse erupts (2023-03-20)
label: verbatim
claim: Quotes Chet Faliszek (Left 4 Dead credit; studio not named in article): "Someone has never sat in on an observed playtest…"; and @AgentDeli, described as a Ubisoft designer: "It's either this or 'the glow' and I promise you when us game developers see the play tests", "people skip over environmentally realistic props", "Unless you guys want a button prompt to 'look at lootables' every time you enter a room". No developer statement uses 'dumb'; that word is only in the article headline, so the 'players are dumb' framing is the press's. Gives no playtest numbers. Tweets as quoted by KYM; tweet pages themselves not opened.

title: GamesRadar interview with Jonathan Dumont, Assassin's Creed Shadows creative director (Ubisoft Quebec), on yellow paint (2025)
read: snippet (GamesRadar page not opened; quote confirmed in 80.lv article citing it, see next row)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary: Dumont said the yellow paint was not in early builds and was added after testers struggled on Hidden Trails activities. Headline wording 'players were really struggling in playtests' matches his quote. Headline framings elsewhere ('stupid players', PC Gamer, VideoGamer) are editorial, not Dumont's.

title: 80.lv, Infamous yellow paint was added to Assassin's Creed Shadows because players were struggling (2025)
label: verbatim
claim: Quotes Dumont (to GamesRadar): "Well, we didn't have it until players were really struggling in playtests to find their path when engaging in hidden trails activity" and "The environment is lush and full, and giving a bit of guidance was needed." Gives no playtest numbers or percentages. Best on-record 'we added it because of playtest data' statement found; it is a qualitative claim, no data shown. Dumont's words do not say players are dumb.

title: GamesRadar (Austin Wood), Witcher 4 design lead Miles Tost on yellow paint, from a PC Gamer interview (2025)
label: developer
claim: Tost: "we're not afraid of adding elements that'll also guide players more directly" (also for accessibility); yellow paint is "one of the many tools", problem is when it does too much; "if you properly weaponise the entire arsenal of your toolkit of guidance as a level designer, then you can subdue each individual element and make it more subtle… the player not noticing the guidance. The strings carefully pulling them along. That is, for me, the sweet spot." Names Uncharted's flags as an in-world alternative: "it fits gently into the environment, as opposed to… someone went into this specific spot and painted a yellow line, because at that point it's not necessarily believable." 'People see through the smoke and mirrors' is Tost's. Not a defence from playtest data; a design-lead view on subtlety. Mentions Witcher 3 added white climb decals. Author's own opinion (most players don't realize how badly they need it) is the journalist's.

title: GamesRadar, Star Wars Outlaws sidesteps RE4 remake and FF7 Rebirth's yellow paint discourse by making it optional
label: snippet
claim: Headline confirms Star Wars Outlaws (Ubisoft Massive) makes the paint optional. Details are in the PC Gamer row below.

title: PC Gamer, Star Wars Outlaws will finally let us turn off that annoying yellow paint on every climbing surface (2024)
read: full (curl, article body; Explorer Mode name and quote text from the writer, not Ubisoft's own post)
label: opinion
claim: Reports Ubisoft Massive's "Explorer Mode" that turns off the "guiding color on core navigational elements" (a yellow-paint toggle). Writer: "developers are often quick to counter this feedback by reminding players that yellow paint is the result of testers getting lost in early playtests"; critique: paint stole "opportunities for players to discover things on their own"; "most videogames don't consider 'searching' to be a skill anymore"; "To play a new game is to learn its language." Writer admits mode was not active in the preview build; he fell to his death once without it. Names alternatives: Half-Life and Portal guiding eyes "with lights, props, and sounds"; Star Wars Jedi: Survivor's visual language (grated metal with round holes = climb, horizontal scratches = wallrun). Rebuttal evidence (does turning it off cost anything) not tested.

title: Search-result summaries on FF7 Rebirth: no toggle found
label: null
claim: Queries: 'Final Fantasy VII Rebirth option disable yellow paint climbing ledges highlights setting'. Result summaries: no toggle for FF7 Rebirth found; Hamaguchi said 'there is definitely a need'; patch 1.020 notes mention improved guidance climbing ivy in Mythril Mine. Kotaku article (fetched) mentions no toggle. Probe could return a toggle (Outlaws surfaced), but I did not read FF7 Rebirth's settings menu or patch notes directly. Horizon, Alan Wake 2 and an RE4 official option not checked; the RE4 remake paint removal is a mod (GamesRadar headline 'Modders are removing the yellow paint', not opened).

title: Kotaku, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth director says there are times when yellow paint is definitely needed (2024)
label: developer
claim: Director Naoki Hamaguchi (Square Enix), to GamesRadar as cited by Kotaku: "there is definitely a need for that kind of thing in a lot of ways" and "there are definitely times where that is needed." No playtest data, no toggle mentioned.

title: GamesRadar (Anne-Marie Ostler), Deathloop and Dishonored developers on guiding players without yellow paint (2024-02)
label: developer
claim: Dinga Bakaba (Deathloop director, Arkane Lyon) via tweet 2024-02-11: avoiding paint marks is "a choice and investment"; alternatives need "a lot of reactive work" after each playtest, "a constant dialog with the playtesters". Thread (by Andrey Mironov, not a Arkane dev) shows: arrows/text that fit the world (Wonder Wheel), a light in a dingy bunker, a light on a safe keypad, sudden loud sounds. Deathloop campaign designer Dana Nightingale: "Details tell a story" (flies over a trash can). A Deathloop level designer (surname Eveillé per article) concedes they used paint too: Colt's apartment ended up with red paint on the wall, a massive spotlight on the window, and a ramp, after "so much difficulties to indicate that place". Journalist's summary: yellow paint isn't necessary but avoiding it is a lot of work. Good counter-example: even the avoid-paint studio needed a stack of cues for one goal.

title: Game Developer, Control Resonant director lays out case for avoiding excessive yellow paint (Mikael Kasurinen on Dropped Frames podcast)
label: developer
claim: Kasurinen: "If it feels like it's like 'go here,' it's not anymore a decision for the player. Somebody already decided for you."; avoiding paint is "a conscious choice"; "nothing better" than finding your own way from A to B; admits risk of the game being "impenetrable"; wants players to ask "did I make the right choice?"; "If you want to get the most out of this world, you have to participate." Article says consistent gravity guides rain/wind direction to keep players oriented. The most direct developer statement of the route-is-the-player's principle; says nothing about playtest data.

title: 80.lv (Arti Sergeev), Defining environment language for video games, on Emilia Schatz (Naughty Dog lead game designer) (2017-06-27)
label: practitioner
claim: Written article, not a recorded talk. "Defined affordances are when the game goes to length to associate arbitrary visuals with in-game mechanics", example "making all climbable handholds painted yellow" (a hypothetical example, not a named game). Schatz favors shape/structure: "The shape and structure in a well-designed level is a subtle means of communicating with the player" plus cultural affordances (stairs, ladders). "Explicit and Defined messaging break immersion and so should be considered a fallback plan." Useful: a Naughty Dog designer's own taxonomy of the options, with paint as the last rung.

title: Engadget, Overheard@GDC: Seeing red in Mirror's Edge (2010)
label: verbatim
claim: Mirror's Edge level designer Elisabetta Silli at GDC: "Red is an odd choice because it means danger or stop." Also "Red is perfect for Faith, I wouldn't change it." Article reports (not quoted) that for a sequel she'd rely less on the red flashes and more on navigation so players know what's coming. Runner vision as precedent: red marks the route objects, in a game built around parkour speed. Does not give playtest data.

title: Milam & El Nasr, Design Patterns to Guide Player Movement in 3D Games (Sandbox@SIGGRAPH, 2010)
read: snippet (search results only; full text not obtained)
label: snippet
claim: Search results say the paper proposes level-design patterns for guiding player movement, built from designer interviews and gameplay analysis, validated by expert review and inter-rater agreement. A later paper (FDG 2014 on 3D adventure games) says these patterns focus on literal visual guidance (Collection, Path Target, Pursue AI, Path Movement and Resistance, Player is Vulnerable) and that its own work targets subtler cues. A companion, 'Analysis of Level Design Push & Pull within 21 games', applies the patterns. I did not read definitions. Not an experiment on yellow paint or on whether players get lost; no evidence in what I saw that lighting or colour cues were tested for effect on behaviour.

title: No controlled study found on yellow paint or on playtest-derived navigation failure rates
label: null
claim: Queries run: 'Resident Evil 4 remake yellow paint developer explains playtesters ledges'; '"yellow paint" video games playtesters get lost developer designer says signposting'; 'Milam El Nasr design patterns player guidance navigation game levels'; plus a pdf query. Nothing peer-reviewed measured the effect of paint on getting lost or on immersion. All 'testers get lost' evidence is developer assertion; no study found with numbers. Not covered: Horizon, Tomb Raider developer statements, Alan Wake 2, Half-Life 2 lighting talk, 'weenie' (Disney) in a games context, RE4 remake Capcom statement.

title: GamesRadar, Debate over RE4 remake's yellow paint resurfaces as devs explain just how much help players really need ('realism is less immersive')
read: snippet (headline + search summary; body not retrieved by fetch or curl)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary says Joseph Hunter (AkaBaka; lead developer of Sucker for Love) said paint came after a playtester struggled for a long stretch; indie dev Rittzler blames the crutch on blockbusters not investing in exploration/puzzles. These are indie devs commenting on someone else's game, not RE4's makers; not verified against the article. Headline fragment 'Realism is less immersive' attributed to a developer without a name.

title: Mirror's Edge Runner Vision coverage (WoLD blog; EA Catalyst post 'Follow the red: Runner's Vision')
label: snippet
claim: Search summary: runner vision tints doors, railings, ledges, pipes and ropes red; a developer interview calls it 'what we call runner vision'; it marks the route objects. Another review says red objects get 'less overt' in later levels. Not opened. Relevant to marking the route versus the goal: runner vision marks the objects that make up the route, not the destination, yet the player still chooses among them.

title: Austin Wood, Debate over Resident Evil 4 Remake's yellow paint resurfaces as devs explain just how much help players really need (GamesRadar, 2023-10-06)
label: practitioner
claim: Quotes developers commenting on others' games. Damion Schubert (Boss Fight): 'the push towards more realistic art increases the need for more unrealistic visual cues'; 'realism is less immersive'; 'Immersion is not a measure of how realistic the grass looks, it's a measure of how much you are into flow'; 'The things that break immersion are the things that break your flow in a game, usually because you know what you need to do but can't figure out how to interact with the game to do it'; 'Trying to open 30 doors to find one we can go through breaks immersion'. David Szymanski: detailed materials make unobtrusive direction harder, devs 'err on the side of caution'. Palle Hoffstein (The Division artist): once thought 'Players aren't stupid. Let them explore', after playtesting 'put it back'. Joseph Hunter (indie, not RE4): paint added after a dev watched a tester stuck 20 minutes. Pedro Braga (Inner Voices, own game, developer): players jumped right into the void until a spinning staircase turned them left; nobody entered village houses until a giant exclamation point; necessary item on a pedestal untaken until floating and glowing; holes impossible to jump made twice as large. Writer's own view (opinion): those who disable it 'deserve the frustration'. No playtest numbers.

title: Pinelle, Wong, Stach, Heuristic Evaluation for Games (CHI 2008)
label: research
claim: Read in full. Method: 108 GameSpot PC game reviews (since 2001, scores <=8.0, 18 per genre x 6 genres, 24 reviewers), coded by 3 researchers into 285 usability problems (2.64/game) in 12 categories, translated into ten heuristics. Category totals: unpredictable response 42; training and help 36 ('A tutorial and a better online manual are sorely needed'); difficult controls 31; timeliness 29; game status info 28 ('The map function reveals everything ... except where you are'); camera 23; AI 22; clumsy input 21; complex command sequences 20; visual representations 16; customization 11; skip content 6. Heuristic 8: 'Provide users with information on game status' (incl. 'objectives'); H9: 'Provide instructions, training, and help' incl. 'default or recommended choices'; H2: 'Allow users to customize video and audio settings, difficulty and game speed'; H6: 'Provide intuitive and customizable input mappings' ('Games should allow users to remap'). Evaluation: 5 evaluators (experienced gamers, formal usability training), one RTS demo (Necromania), ~90 min, 45 problems; H9 most used (12, mean severity 3.30), H8 10; evaluator quote 'No help system or tutorial. Still don't understand what I'm supposed to be doing.' Stated limits: only 5 evaluators and one game, 'additional testing' needed; PC single-player commercial games only; reviewers 'not usability professionals', 'more subtle design problems were missed'; no engagement/fun coverage; heuristics may narrow evaluators' focus. Bearing on the rule: 'review current objectives / what to do next' SUPPORTED indirectly (H8 lists objectives; evaluator could not tell what to do) but paper has no 'what to do next' category and no unlock-goal category; 'unlock condition shown as readable goal before meeting it' NOT ADDRESSED (no hidden-unlock or hidden-information category; closest is category 8 inadequate status info); 'controls customisable' SUPPORTED (H6, category 6); 'settings remembered' NOT ADDRESSED (H2 is about availability of settings, not persistence); customization had only 11 of 285 problems. Evidence is expert-inspection from reviews, not player testing.

title: Milam, Seif El Nasr, Design Patterns to Guide Player Movement in 3D Games (Sandbox 2010)
label: research
claim: Descriptive pattern taxonomy, not a player test. Five patterns: Collect ("incentivizes and rewards items placed around the level"), Path Target ("orients and directs player movement or attention towards visible targets"; e.g. a "visible landmark to attract movement", "Visible points along a path are used in a similar way as wayfinding signage"), Pursue AI, Path Movement and Resistance ("general narrative goal for the player to continue through a linear mission/quest"; goal can be near and "visual, e.g., a lighthouse" as in MOH bunker, or "abstract" as FEAR 'Go to the Data Center' reached via corridors and enemy resistance), Player Vulnerable. Games: BioShock, F.E.A.R. Perseus Mandate, Lost Via Domus, Medal of Honor 2. Method: emailed AAA designers, "four responses" (one per game), 1-hour interviews after researcher played first hours; one researcher derived patterns from interview examples and video-coded six play sessions; face validity = designers agreed patterns "certainly valid"; reliability = two researchers coded ~20 min of Assassin's Creed (not one of the analysed games), kappa .363 (Path Target goal, lowest) to .699; "fair, moderate and substantial agreement in 9 out of 12 occurrences of 4 out of 5 patterns"; Collection never occurred. Authors' stated limit: future work to "validate this model with several other games and input from other designers". Nothing on players getting lost, no cold testers, no explicit-vs-subtle comparison; one designer only says patterns work "explicitly when tied to objectives and implicitly" to "subtlety nudge". Goal vs route is not separated as marking problem: the paper says Path Movement goal can be deliberately abstract, so 'always mark the goal' is qualified by design choice. Bearing on the rule: neither supports nor contradicts; at most consonant with landmarks-as-wayfinding, no evidence on toggles or fallback ordering.
